question_text: A 48-hour-old newborn presents in respiratory distress. He is gasping for breath in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) and has had a fever for the past 2 days with a temperature ranging between 37.2°C (99.0°F) and 38.6°C (101.5°F). He also has not been feeding well and seems to be lethargic. The patient was delivered normally at 36 weeks of gestation. His mother had a premature rupture of membranes, which occurred with her last pregnancy, as well. No history of infection during pregnancy. On physical examination, a bulging anterior fontanelle is noticed, along with tensing of the extensor muscles. A lumbar puncture is performed, and CSF analysis is pending. Which of the following would be the best course of treatment in this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 48-hour-old newborn presents in respiratory distress. He is gasping for breath in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) and has had a fever for the past 2 days with a temperature ranging between 37.2°C (99.0°F) and 38.6°C (101.5°F). He also has not been feeding well and seems to be lethargic. The patient was delivered normally at 36 weeks of gestation. His mother had a premature rupture of membranes, which occurred with her last pregnancy, as well. No history of infection during pregnancy. On physical examination, a bulging anterior fontanelle is noticed, along with tensing of the extensor muscles. A lumbar puncture is performed, and CSF analysis is pending. Which of the following would be the best course of treatment in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Ampicillin and gentamicin
opb. Ampicillin and cefotaxime
opc. Ampicillin and acyclovir
opd. Ampicillin and ticarcillin
ope. Ampicillin and sulbactam

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 48-hour-old newborn presents with respiratory distress, fever, lethargy, and a bulging anterior fontanelle, indicating a high suspicion for meningitis or sepsis, particularly given the history of premature rupture of membranes. The presence of fever and lethargy suggests a systemic infection, and the bulging fontanelle indicates possible increased intracranial pressure, which is consistent with meningitis. Empirical treatment for suspected bacterial meningitis in neonates typically includes Ampicillin combined with a third-generation cephalosporin like cefotaxime, which covers common pathogens such as Group B Streptococcus and E. coli. While Ampicillin and gentamicin are also used for early-onset sepsis, cefotaxime is preferred for meningitis due to its broader coverage of potential pathogens. Therefore, the best course of treatment is Ampicillin and cefotaxime, aligning with current medical consensus on managing suspected neonatal meningitis.
